sn2.1:1.3: The commentary says that godlings (_devaputta_) are born “in the lap of the gods”, that is, not from a womb. Typically, in contrast with the “deities” (_devatā_), they are named individuals. The commentary also takes the term as gendered, with _devaputta_ as “son of god” and _devadhītā_ as “daughter of god”. But as the latter term is not attested in early Pali (or Sanskrit) we should probably take _devaputta_ as gender-neutral (like _devatā_). This is supported by pre-Buddhist Sanskrit, where we only find _devaputra_ as an adjective, “the heaven and earth, whose children are gods”. At Rig Veda 1.185.4, those children are “two young women, sisters”. | It is not clear who this “Kassapa” is, but perhaps he is the Vedic sage of that name.
sn2.1:1.4: This is an unusual thing to say, as the Buddha obviously gave instructions for mendicants very often. It must have a specific context; the commentarial explanation relies on a much later mythology. | This suggests that the verse below, which is phrased as a direct exhortation to the mendicants, is to be read as the godling quoting the Buddha’s own words. However, no such verse is attributed to the Buddha in the Pali canon.
sn2.1:2.1: I read _sikkhetha_ as second person plural optative, and _subhāsitassa_ (etc.) as dative (of purpose), although we would expect the _āya_ form in this sense. The commentary glosses with third singular and accusative (_subhāsitaṁ sikkheyya_). Norman (*Elders Verses I*, note 239) suggests it may be locative.
